summary: Provides a general framework for describing network traffic flows and presents an architecture for measuring and reporting them. It explains how this fits into an overall flow architecture and how it can be used on the Internet. This is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the blueprint for a system that counts the data cars on the Internet's roads and reports the totals.

subtitle: A blueprint for measuring network traffic by grouping packets into flows, using meters, readers and managers.

tldr.problem: Network operators need comparable data on how traffic is used, for planning, performance and attributing usage to users, across many protocols and platforms.
tldr.mechanism: Meters sort observed packets into flows using user-written rule sets and keep counts in a flow table. Meter readers collect that data and managers configure both.
tldr.outcome: This informational memo is an architecture, not a protocol, and it replaces RFC 2063. Transport, security and data formats are left to other documents.

today: RFC 2722 is an Informational memo that obsoletes RFC 2063, and no later RFC is listed as replacing it. It works alongside the Meter MIB (RFC 2720) and the SRL rule language (RFC 2723).

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
This memo describes an architecture for measuring and reporting traffic flows on data networks. Its goals are that the flow model applies to any protocol using address attributes at the adjacent, network and transport layers, that attributes are valid across protocol stacks, that users pick what to collect by writing rule sets, and that data reduction happens as close to the measurement point as possible.

It lists uses for the resulting data: understanding existing networks, planning growth, quantifying performance, verifying service quality and attributing usage to users. It is explicitly not a protocol specification. It structures the information a measurement system must collect, states requirements, and outlines trade-offs. Billing and tariff questions are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal is one shared way of counting traffic, so different networks can compare their numbers.

sections.title: Meters, Readers, Managers and Applications
sections.content:
The model has four kinds of parts. A meter sits at a measurement point, watches packets pass, classifies them into groups and accumulates counts such as packets and bytes. A meter reader collects the resulting usage data. A manager configures meters and controls meter readers. An analysis application turns usage data into reports such as traffic flow matrices.

Several relationships are spelled out. A meter reader can read from one or more meters, with no need to synchronize collections. A meter reader may be controlled by only a single manager. One manager should be the master of a meter and alone set meter-wide parameters such as sampling. Redundant meters and readers can improve reliability: if one of two readers fails, the other keeps collecting.

Sampling is not prescribed. The memo says careful meters compress data well enough that sampling is seldom needed on typical LANs and WANs, and that any sampling used should not bias results.
sections.plainLanguage: A meter is the counter at the roadside, the reader goes round collecting the tallies, the manager tells them both what to do, and the analyst writes the report.

sections.title: Flows, Attributes and Granularity
sections.content:
A traffic flow is described as an artificial logical equivalent to a call or connection: a portion of traffic, delimited by start and stop times, that belongs to one metered traffic group. Because IP is connectionless, the meter uses its rules to decide which flow each packet belongs to.

Each flow record holds attributes: source and destination addresses (interface, adjacent, peer and transport, each with a mask), first and last times, forward and backward counts of packets and bytes, and other attributes such as the rule set number. Naming only a source address, for example, counts all packets to and from that address.

Granularity is the control knob trading detail against overhead. Coarser means more aggregation and fewer flows to store. It is set by the metered traffic group, how packets are categorized and flow lifetime, all via the current rule set.

The memo recommends rolling counters, which keep counting in the same flow record after a report, so that lost reports can be recovered. The flow start time tells a continuing flow from a new one. Each packet is counted in at most one flow per running rule set, so overlapping totals need separate buckets or separate rule sets.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is one conversation between two places. You can count each conversation separately or lump many together, depending on how much detail you want.

sections.title: How a Meter Handles Packets
sections.content:
For each packet header, the meter builds a match key and passes it to the Packet Matching Engine (PME), a virtual machine whose program is the current rule set. The result is ignore, no match, or success with a flow key that locates or creates the flow's record in the flow table.

Because flows are bidirectional, the meter tries to match the packet one way and, if that fails, in the reverse direction, then counts it as forward or reverse traffic. This means rule sets must be consistent: counting A to B but ignoring B to A is given as an example of a bad rule set. The memo suggests writing rules that classify only the forward direction.

Each rule has a test (attribute & mask = value) and an action (an opcode plus a parameter). The memo defines 17 opcodes, including Ignore, NoMatch, Count, Gosub and PushRuleTo. Rule set 1 is built into the meter and cannot change, and a task given rule set 0 stops measuring.
sections.plainLanguage: For each packet, the meter checks a list of rules like a checklist and decides: skip it, or add one to this conversation's tally.

sections.title: The Flow Table and Managing Load
sections.content:
The flow table holds flow records, each in one of three states: INACTIVE (unused), CURRENT (in use and recently seen) or IDLE (no packets for the meter's inactivity time). New flows take an inactive record first, otherwise an idle one. Idle records are recovered, ideally after every registered reader has collected them, and the meter drops readers that miss their timeout.

When memory use rises above a high-water mark, the meter should switch to a coarser standby rule set to slow the creation of new flows. A manager can then poll more often or later switch back. The meter might also send a trap or dump data to a reader. Managers also handle outages of meters, readers and managers, and the memo suggests standard rule sets by protocol type, adjacent systems, end systems, transport type, or hybrids.

Meter readers store usage records, listing packet and byte counts per flow, in flow data files. How data moves from meter to reader is not specified. SNMP with the Meter MIB is given as one example.
sections.plainLanguage: If the meter's notebook fills up, it switches to rougher counting. The manager can also ask the collectors to come by more often.

sections.title: Threats and Countermeasures
sections.content:
The memo lists four threats: attempts to disable a meter (for instance by sending packets to many addresses to inflate the flow table and force the coarser standby rule set), unauthorized use of system resources, unauthorized disclosure of data, and unauthorized alteration, replacement or destruction of data.

The first cannot be completely countered, but the memo advises giving a meter three or more times the flow memory it normally needs and collecting often. The others call for authentication and access control, confidentiality and integrity services respectively. Elements that intercommunicate should authenticate mutually and check access, and transfers should be integrity-protected. The memo recommends strong cryptography but does not specify security protocols, leaving them to the management and collection protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could try to flood the counter or fake the numbers, so the pieces should check each other's identity and protect their messages.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PARTS OF THE MEASUREMENT MODEL

items.title: Meter
items.text: Observes packets at a measurement point and accumulates flow data.

items.title: Meter reader
items.text: Collects usage data from meters for analysis applications.

items.title: Manager
items.text: Configures meters and controls meter readers.

items.title: Analysis application
items.text: Turns usage data into reports such as traffic flow matrices.

items.label: Ignore
items.desc: Stop matching; the packet is not counted.

items.label: NoMatch
items.desc: Stop matching with failure; may be retried with addresses reversed.

items.label: Count
items.desc: Stop matching and build a flow key from the pattern queue.

items.label: CountPkt
items.desc: Like Count, but saves the masked packet header value.

items.label: Gosub
items.desc: Call a subroutine and set the test indicator.

items.label: GosubAct
items.desc: Like Gosub, with the test indicator cleared.

items.label: Assign
items.desc: Set the rule's attribute to the parameter value.

items.label: AssignAct
items.desc: Like Assign, with the test indicator cleared.

items.label: GotoAct
items.desc: Like Goto, with the test indicator cleared.

items.label: PushRuleTo
items.desc: Save the rule's attribute, mask and value in the pattern queue.

items.label: PushRuleToAct
items.desc: Like PushRuleTo, with the test indicator cleared.

items.label: PushPktTo
items.desc: Save the masked packet header value in the pattern queue.

items.label: PushPktToAct
items.desc: Like PushPktTo, with the test indicator cleared.

items.label: PopTo
items.desc: Delete the most recent pattern queue item.

items.label: PopToAct
items.desc: Like PopTo, with the test indicator cleared.

transitions.label: record reused for a new flow
